Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained significant interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a new contrastive loss function. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data points gives it an advantage over existing methods. Our framework further demonstrates feature extraction capabilities without the need for external labels, with the option to incorporate supervised learning using existing methods. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through various feature extraction tasks across six datasets, showing superior performance in similar and similar+dissimilar contrastive learning scenarios, and comparable results in supervised feature extraction scenarios.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance in terms of prediction accuracy and variable selection is par with the best possible approach and outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in most scenarios. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the two-step algorithm enhances the Group Lasso's interpretability.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge graph Wikibpedia outperforms the baseline in various benchmarks, including the one designed by Wang et al. (2022), especially when working with larger model sizes and more extensive knowledge graphs. Furthermore, we find that this technique enhances the performance of zero-shot prompt-based methods and leads to meaningful improvements in task-specific settings, including the creation of a pair of datasets to compare one trained on structured knowledge versus plain text, resulting in a 11% average gain in accuracy across multiple models. We also show that models trained using our technique excel in sophisticated reasoning, including the ability to perform single and multi-hop inference on the CogNeo knowledge graph in a completely settings-natural manner in comparison to traditional fine-tuning approaches.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present study outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristics of convection for extended vertical domain simulations where all air parcels do not revert to their original state at the ground level.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
Analyzing public sentiment is also essential in forecasting and managing social unrest.
Although numerous studies have analyzed sentiment on Twitter using various techniques,
no study has explicitly investigated the ability of Recurrent Neural Network models to
assess public sentiment. In this paper, we evaluate the capability of a Recurrent Neural
Network model, specifically a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, to analyze
sentiment on Twitter. We discover that an LSTM network can effectively analyze
sentiment on Twitter and outperforms traditional methods such as Naive Bayes and
Support Vector Machines. We also compare the An LSTM model to variant an LSTM network
network architectures to determine the areas for optimization.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions under which an light ring phase transition occurs, marking a shift from short to long distance behavior. This occurrence is tied to non-monotonic behavior in light radius with varying scalar carding parameter, leading to attractive and repulsive forces that influence orbiting black hole particles. Moreover, we investigate how the shadow radius changes in relation to non-dimensional charge and angular momentum, as well as their impact on black hole image magnification and distortion. Additionally, we study the link between the light ring phase transition and van der Waals (VDW) like behavior in charged AdS black hole, discovering that the region of light ring attraction overlaps with the VDW phase transition region. However, we note that the shadow radius becomes ineffective at detecting non-monotonic behavior in rotating black holes due to angular momentum influence.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, it is necessary to foresee where a viewer will look. Prior
research on viewport prediction for VR videos was conducted for linear videos
with fixed views. However, in custom 360-degree videos, eye movement prediction
is more complex due to fixed focal points and sudden shifts to areas outside
the initial content's focal range. In order to adapt existing eye prediction
techniques to these custom videos, we analyzed in detail eye loss and focal
loss from subtitle information. As a result, a new model was developed using
data from existing subtitle viewers to accurately predict a viewer's viewport.
Experimental results show that this approach can significantly increase the
video's useful area and expand the visible frame, thereby improving overall
content visibility and minimization video data requirements while maintaining
content visibility.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling thermal equilibrium conditions and thermal dynamic processes for one-dimensional systems. These techniques approximate condition numbers of complex statistical mechanics expressions, which have subsequently been squared in determining thermally averaged quantities. This study restructures the relevant expressions using orthogonal factorizations, circumventing an estimation of the complex diagonal elements, which are typically assumed to be accurately represented in existing methods, but may not necessarily hold near system boundaries in some cases, including the application of the thermal matrix product state and the stochastic thermal tensor network in recent studies, and often are not explicitly calculated in the recent study's algorithms. Moreover, the replacement of direct sampling of state amplitudes with locally accurate estimations of randomly generated random numbers enhances the efficiency of current algorithms by at least a constant factor of one million in some instances, which also shifts the source of potential inaccuracies to the network's tail, which can be effectively mitigated through the application of simple and highly efficient variations that retain the primary characteristics of the original methods.

We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$.

Researchers are focusing on extremely thin alloys made of rare earth and transition metals, with controlled composition and unique magnetic properties, to create advanced photonic applications that operate rapidly. Despite the potential, it is very difficult to achieve small scale dimensions, which are essential for scaling down devices, while maintaining the necessary properties for a long duration. This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating these materials into extremely thin crystal structures that manipulate light, retaining their properties for an extended period. The designed micro-surface crystal structure works in conjunction with the unique magnetic properties of the alloy to exhibit extremely fast switching capabilities and highly variable color reflection characteristics. This breakthrough enables rare earth and transition metal alloys to be used in innovative magnetic light control technologies, including very small scale applications.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on the teacher model and training data being available. This paper explores an alternative approach, in which the teacher model remains inaccessible, but a pre-trained model can make binary classifications correctly. We investigate a scenario where both models lack explicit access to the input labels. Our innovative design enables simultaneous learning by the student and supervisor, allowing them to improve their mutual performance. This simultaneous learning strategy is demonstrated to be more effective than when the student is trained independently with access to the input labels. Furthermore, this approach is particularly beneficial in cases when the student model was trained using a suboptimal network structure. Both qualitative and quantitative results, using decision-based knowledge distillation, support the findings of this research.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the sum of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ and $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*+} K^-`` decays is estimated at (2.7±0.4±0.3±0.2) ×10^-4.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules over specific rings, particularly those that are multilinear over $K[x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n]$ when $K$ is a field with characteristic zero, we can determine that these modules often have submodules with no repetition, and there is a one-to-one correspondence between them and the set of semistandard Young tableaux of a particular shape. Using the properties of these Young tableaux, we can determine the lattice of submodules for these modules in a straightforward combinatorial way, and as a result, we can also determine that modules with no repetition correspond to affine semigroups when the characteristic of the field is not four, or to lattices of varieties when the characteristic is zero.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert feedback is often impractical due to its expensive and inconsistent nature. In this work, we introduce a novel approach known as Co-Imitation Learning, which leverages the interplay between policy gradient methods and behavior learning from peer agents. By learning from neighboring agents in the state-space, we aim to minimize the distribution gap between the agent being trained and its peers, thereby facilitating faster convergence and performance improvements. To realize this concept, we develop an algorithm employing online representative agents and employ a conditionally undifferentiable imitation loss function. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the concept of cooperative guidance's ability to accelerate convergence and performance gains. To validate our approach, we conduct both numerical simulations and real-world experiments, comparing COIL with conventional RL methods and demonstrating its superior convergence rate and performance.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polar codes. Utilizing the new metric, we demonstrate its effectiveness through comparisons with the existing distance function and simulate successful PAC code decoding with low-computation schemes, achieving error rates comparable to conventional polar codes at much higher error rates.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement.

because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment.

We explore how several established and established theorems regarding biharmonic hypersurfaces can be stated using recurrent operators in two aspects. Furthermore, we establish a specific result stating that if a hypersurface within a Euclidean environment is found to have a specific property related to a function $\lambda$, it is considered minimal due to its biharmonic nature. This particular issue has been addressed by distinguishing the research of various authors, with research from K. Koufogiorgos and E. Papantoniou being particularly relevant.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019).

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregated data. 
Recently, a reverse engineering approach has been proposed to uncover the hidden geometry of such complex networks by comparing their observed statistics with those generated random models and identifying the most matching model as an indicator of the underlying structure. 
Using this method, the geometry of complex assemblies of nanoscale magnetic materials, specifically 3D blocks composed of cubic grains, has been analyzed. 
These blocks exhibit varying interaction patterns - random, face-based, and diagonal - and their resulting magnetic reversals provide evidence for the disclosed hidden geometries. 
Our study demonstrates that ensemble and individual dynamics of these assemblies, in terms of temperature and field-induced spin-flip thresholds, offer crucial insights for designing advanced nanodevice applications. 
Furthermore, the combination of cubic symmetry and strong exchange interactions, resulting in a 3D arrangement of nanocubes, has been shown to offer unique potential for developing robust nanodevice technology.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the number of protons being released. Combining the data from all four trips, we found the average solar wind energy flux that made it into the innermost space over a wide range of values was about 4 ergs per second per square meter, but we noticed some of the higher energy ranges got stuck getting the same readings over and over, likely because they came from the same area of the sun and got trapped. We noted that the energy ranges we found were quite broad, and we found the readings often spiked to much higher levels for long periods of time, which were caused by events occurring deep in the inner solar system that could last quite far and could get reflected off the same areas over and over, and we saw the close approaches to the earth and what the Parker Solar Probe recorded lined up quite well with one another.

Thanks to speech emotion recognition's emotional intelligence, it can be used in
important areas like customer service and mental health analysis. Although SER has
made significant progress in theoretical research, it lags behind in real-world
applications due to its inability to accurately identify emotions in speech from
newly encountered domains. This inaccuracy is largely caused by the characteristic
patterns learned neural networks, which differ from human emotional expression
expression and are heavily influenced by the specific domain they were trained on.
This paper introduces a new approach called Deep Reinforcement Learning Based
Domain Adaptation speech emotion recognition, which efficiently adapts neural
network-based SER models to new domains with limited labeled data while also
improving robustness and reducing model overfitting. To validate the proposed
method, an experimental analysis was conducted on multiple datasets, comparing
its performance to that of conventional classification neural networks. The
experimental results show that the proposed DRLDA framework consistently
outperforms conventional neural network-based adaptation strategies across various
target domains, effectively enhancing the emotion-ignorance, robustness, and
overall speech emotion recognition accuracy.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$. The resulting rate is fit with CLN and BGL form factor parametrisations to derive key parameters for both models.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen periodic functions, and and then expanded upon through exponential and polynomial components. This class of polynomial-phase functions can be utilized to describe the well-known Airy and Bessel functions, as well as an expansion of the semi-classical limit, and ultimately leads to an explicit, closed-form expression.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic, a new model was developed to allocate social mobility-driven benefits optimally across generations. The research reveals that allocating benefits uniformly across generations isn't always the most beneficial approach. Instead, rising the economic status of a generation might warrant compensating them with fewer benefits to help those starting at a disadvantageous position. Moreover, due to its drive social mobility, the model indicates that compensating disadvantaged individuals with more than their fair share can be advantageous. However, under certain conditions revealed by the research, allocating benefits uniformly across generations may be beneficial despite its limitations.

In 2015, the CERN synchrotron light source upgrade project introduced a new way to measure electron beam sizes in horizontal and vertical dimensions using "lambda" scans. These scans rely on a specific effect called beam-beam displacement, which occurs when a beam synchrotron extracts photons from a target. A 3D model of this effect's geometry was created to accurately analyze the results. The analysis also took into account the influence of two other factors: "emittance crossing" and "coupling", which can also affect the number of photons produced. The findings indicated that this method offers accurate measurements of beam sizes, particularly for small beams used in direct electron applications.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data files in the format required by several upcoming sensitive experiments, including the CMB-S4 small-scale detectors, S-4 polarised camera of the Chinese space station lunar surface experiment, and Simons Observatory. The tool also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects in its simulated data files. This article provides potential limitations in accurately modelling instrumental systematic effects and discusses the necessary future enhancements to achieve precise model of such effects. Providing accurate and consistent simulated inclusive datasets will be crucial for the successful analysis of upcoming sensitive experiments' massive data sets.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces the CSDNetwork architecture, which fuses spatial and frequency domain features to facilitate accurate detection. Furthermore, we refine this model to accommodate multi-classification challenges in cross-stitching tasks by incorporating a novel frequency attention mechanism and modifying the parameter sharing strategy, resulting in the MD-CSDNetwork framework. Both simulated and real-world experiments conducted on FaceForeniscs++ and Fooseface datasets validate our hypothesis and demonstrate the superiority of our model over existing methods in the cross-stitching domain, yielding precise detection scores of 0.820 and 0.948, respectively.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any non-zero ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ in the ring of integers of $K$, the norm satisfies the bound $N(\mathfrak{a}) \leq (c_K + o(1)) (\log N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\mathfrak{a}))^{(n-1)/2}$, where $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}$ denotes the standard norm, and $c_K$ is a constant dependent on $K$. Furthermore, for the first two successive minima $\lambda_{1}(\lambda)$ and $\lambda_{2}(\lambda)$ of an order $\lambda$ in $K$, the following inequality holds: $\lambda_{1}(\lambda)\lambda_{2}(\lambda) \leq (c_K + o(1)) \log^{(n-1)/2}(|\det(\lambda)|)^{(n-1)/2}$, where $\det(\lambda)$ is the volume of the fundamental domain of the lattice associated with the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$. These findings are connected to the geometry of numbers and have implications for the study of ideal classes and lattice packings in high-dimensional spaces.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract and easily traceable. Forsage's extraordinary success saw it become one of the most downloaded and viewed YouTube presentations by their promoters. With its code publicly accessible, researchers and others examined the Forsage scheme's characteristics, its user base's geographic distribution, the amounts transferred between users, the timing of transactions, the scheme's sudden cessation, and its global impact. The implications of this study are broad, offering valuable insights for analyzing future pyramid schemes until decentralized platforms make such schemes traceable in the future.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous sources such as background stars and foreground objects. We estimate the minimum light reduction these clusters cause and calculated their distances from Earth, total brightness, movement through space, metal composition, and age. We discovered that most proposed clusters exhibited typical motion patterns consistent with the galaxy's disk, although some showed metal compositions and ages that diverged significantly from expected values for globular clusters. We also compared our results with previously established globular clusters in the galaxy and determined that the majority of objects under investigation cannot be classified as globular clusters based on their chemical composition and age characteristics, thus expanding the known range of globular clusters in the galaxy's disk. We also analyzed the relationship between metal composition and a measure of intrinsic stellar variability known as the period of light oscillation in each object, contributing to a comprehensive understanding of intrinsic variability in objects within the galaxy's bulge with diverse metal compositions.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, and serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss. A key aspect of these networks is their ability to preserve information across different scales, and we classify networks with this property into two subcategories: those that preserve information sharply and those that do so more gradually. We then focus on one type of network structure, called hyper-variable Holographic Multiscale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz, and demonstrate its ability to solve problems related to lossy data transmission and information preservation. Furthermore, we provide concrete methods for creating networks that solve these problems effectively, and for those that do so gradually, we propose an improved design and pattern for a specific network code, with higher efficiency than existing solutions.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process instance, determining the ideal event prediction
point. Our experiments provide valuable insights into selecting the most
effective model architecture and determining when to make predictions most
accurately.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions in both time and frequency domains. It is established that S_1^0 (R_n) contains non-zero functions, while it is shown that S^0 (R_n) and S_1^1 (R_n) consist entirely of complex functions. Furthermore, specific conditions under which these spaces remain invariant under the Fourier transform are determined. Additionally, we determine precise conditions for the image of these spaces under Toeplitz operators to be included in their original form.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions like Kepler, K2, and TESS. To interpret these observations, a comprehensive understanding of white-light stellar flares is necessary. A significant part of a white-light flare's energy occurs in the near-ultraviolet spectrum, which is key to explaining how they affect nearby planets. A detailed model of this near-ultraviolet light must consider both bright stellar flare patches and the dark regions around them. A prominent example, the 1985 April 12 superflare on AD Leo, was analyzed using available near-ultraviolet data, which helped to create and test a model. A photoelectric model based on local thermodynamic equilibrium accurately represented a significant portion of the flare patches and the star's disk. The 24 nearest UV filters' observations matched the model well, except for one filter's anomalous reading. A black body model offered a less accurate explanation, poorly matching the flank signal and filter observations. AD Leo's flare produced highly energetic near-ultraviolet radiation, with a significant amount of extreme near-ultraviolet light. A similar or greater level of energy was found in other large flares on AD Leo. A comprehensive study of white-light flares must consider their associated near-ultraviolet effects.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: rotational, shear, and scaling changes. Next, we outline an general approach utilizing a unique loss function and optimizer to find the most minimal smoothing strategy. Finally, we demonstrate this method's versatility by adapting it to handle all three common three-dimensional transformations. Our results show that TPC outperforms leading techniques by a substantial margin, as evidenced in various point cloud applications such as classification, regression, and detection with distinct performance improvements.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient, sparsely-based adversarial training but also enhance overall generation performance. Experiments on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved results, particularly in terms of sequence generation quality metrics such as BLEU scores.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of these studies is spatial capture-recapture models, which use encounter data to estimate animal density and detectability.  Combining these two types of data can provide more accurate estimates of resource selection and animal density while considering variation in detectability across different spaces.  A new statistical model has been developed to integrate independent encounter and telemetry data for this purpose.  The model handles telemetry data that may contain false positives and accounts for varying detection probabilities in both data sets across space.  It also estimates how environmental variables affect animal encounters and telemetry selections to capture-recapture models.  The proposed model has been validated through a simulation study and applied to estimate animal density and resource selection functions using an urban wild dog population.  The results highlight areas that animals frequently visit around den sites and affect detection probabilities varying across space.  The model produced density estimates comparable to previous studies but with higher uncertainty.  Overall, the new integrated model offers a comprehensive framework for analyzing animal population data in relation to space and resource use.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To address this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine the stability of phase currents in multilayer networks, a parameter otherwise difficult to calculate. This method yields precise results and can be easily applied to higher-order multilayer networks. As an illustration, we analyze a set of connected ring-like multilayer networks and develop a model for the evolution of these systems by incorporating parameter variation over time. This model enables us to investigate the dynamics of a continuous spectrum of oscillating multilayer networks. Furthermore, we propose a mechanism for synchronizing such networks through a broadcasting strategy based on state-dependent control, which ensures global asymptotic stability regardless of the specific multilayer topology in use.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions and the corresponding balance differential operator is well-established.  In the context of the Cauchy stress operator, this process is intricately linked to the topological properties of the underlying manifold's boundary.  This paper delves into the cauchy stress operator's fundamental properties from first principles, identifying its essential characteristics and compatible conditions in both local and global frameworks.  Notably, we have been able to ascertain that in the local framework, the cauchy stress operator can be parameterized using 14 independent components, an improvement upon the previously known 18-component parameterization.  This enhanced understanding has practical applications in the formulation of well-posed compatibly constrained stress problems and the development of stress-driven physics-informed machine learning methods.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software. This endeavor also aligns with the geometric nature of software, where each function is like a shape that changes over time and across different inputs, much akin to continuous software. Our research connects this analogy by establishing a foundation for developing reliable software through the geometry of test functions. This approach leverages the properties of shapes to guarantee accurate software and guides in selecting suitable tests to ensure correct software behavior. Moreover, this framework leads to the development of invariants related to the geometry of software, which can be used to enhance reliability. Our related work suggests that this concept of software as a shape is related to the consistency between code and tests. This novel perspective opens up opportunities to apply proven techniques from topology and algebraic topology to the realm of software testing.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. The group $G_{\text{sc}}(\Phi_0, K)$ is then described as acting on the set containing elements of the form $e_\alpha$, with the condition that the angle between $\alpha$ and $\delta$ is $\frac{\pi}{3}$.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate within a constant factor, specifically in the range of [0.99, 1.01], using n^(log_3 (2)) bits of randomness and low-cost operations resulting in log log_3 (2) rounds and an output of O(log n). The concept of sparse complexity is defined based on the average node degree exceeding a low threshold of d > 2. The established limits demonstrate the difficulty of this problem, indicating that determining the network size is inherently challenging. The initial results indicate that even the simplest approach, two approaches being inclusive of complete and partial connectivity, cannot be effectively solved in two rounds unless the size of the untrusted node collection is unrestricted. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration.

We provide a detailed explanation for a part of Serre's conjecture related to GL_2 through Kummer theory, thereby bypassing the reliance on p-adic Hodge theory. This involves utilizing descriptions of crystalline extension reductions, Kummer theory, Abrashkin's findings, local class field theory, Dembele-Diamond-Roberts' earlier work, Brueckner-Shaferevich-Vostokov's reciprocity laws and their implications to describe and calculate certain G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles.

We establish a precise result for optimal solutions in an isoperimetric problem outside a confined object within the scenario where a large amount of space is considered, denoted as the 'large volume regime.' This achievement comes from a deeper examination of a specific surface-related problem that includes an unknown boundary, both within the confined object and at an infinitely distant point. The analysis involves the discovery of a specific term in an equation, termed 'isoperimetric residue,' which helps in expanding an isoperimetric problem equation when the 'large volume regime' is approached. A key component of the study on these'residues' is a newly introduced flatness standard for surface types that have restricted average curvature and can be used to better understand optimal solutions both qualitatively and quantitatively.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering structures. One such nanofiller, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), not only strengthen the material but also enable the detection of structural issues through changes in electrical conductivity and electrical impedance patterns. This study utilized carbon nanotube-filled epoxy and monitored structural defects through B-sensing, by relying on changes in impedance and image processing techniques. CNT composites were subjected to deliberate damage through indentation, and changes in their conductivity and impedance were analyzed in relation to damage severity and location. By integrating B-sensing technology with a forward model that accounts for sensor electrical networks, the study was able to accurately predict the extent of material cracking. A non-linear mathematical expression was found to describe the relationship between material damage and electrical network behavior with remarkable precision, and a genetic algorithm was used to determine the extent of material failure. This method outperformed traditional statistical approaches in accuracy and efficiency. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of CNT composites in identifying internal material issues through the B-sensing method and a data-driven algorithm.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a parallel between brain neurons and societal individuals, inquiring whether collective intelligence requires individual intellect and what specific forms of individual knowledge contribute to greater collective insight. By integrating principles from connectionism, agent-based modeling, group psychology, economics, and physics, we reframe these concepts through the lens of changing system dynamics. Ultimately, we apply this understanding to explain the coexistence of prey and predator species in the Lotka-Volterra model and the catastrophic consequences of particular individual intellect applications.

This work proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector integrand identities proved using this framework.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain duration after the big bang. During this model's range, the particles' unusual behavior is explained as a result of the scalar field's impact on the previously thought impossible early universe, thus enabling its range to be considered long-lasting despite its short-term instability. The range's duration is governed by its mass, which is believed to be between 10 keV and 1 MeV, offering an opportunity to conduct laboratory-based searches for this scalar particle, even though it may be classified as dark matter, it could leave observable imprints in various cosmological and astrophysical phenomena. Consequently, the scalar range's existence might be detected through modifications in neutrino behavior, anomalies in the decay of massive stars, or the radiation emitted during the early universe.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within a specific region, its conformal blocks can be effectively approximated by a sum of components whose coefficients satisfy an anholomorphic version of the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda conformal field theory's classical equations of motion. This document delves further into the anholomorphic geometry of the Toda conformal blocks for $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ by calculating the first non-trivial correlation functions that reveal their anholomorphic structural properties. We identify and analyze the Ancestor operator responsible for this behavior and present an anholomorphic method for extracting its primary field's null vector. Additionally, we present an explicit, partially solved integral representation for the corresponding conformal block's solution.
We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery, but there's a growing interest in incorporating BCIs to assist with lower limb mobility. To explore this possibility, researchers are using simulated leg movement scenarios, but lack of data on how individuals would actually walk in real life limits the validity of these studies. Real-world walking involves naturally modulating limb movements based on task requirements, but also step-by-step variations that could be automatically identified and decoded from neural activity. Our study investigates the decoding of walking-related brain activity, specifically the state of the current step, the phase of the gait cycle, and step rate, using electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals. Participants performed Treadmill-Based Gait Training (TBGT) while we recorded their brain activity, which was later used to decode step state classification, phase regression, and step rate modulation. Our results show that step state classification can be achieved with high accuracy, particularly for distinguishing the swing phase, and that TBGBT may impair the ability to decode phase and step rate signals. These findings highlight the need to refine simulated movement scenarios to better reflect the complexity of natural walking movements in real-world settings.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity patterns in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing time-series data as observed nodes in dynamic models presents significant challenges, mainly due to the need to integrate classification networks with long short-term memory components, which compromises efficiency and scalability. In contrast, we introduce a novel and streamlined approach by employing a simple recurrent model to process flattened edge features, which significantly enhances the estimation of representation-based graph neural models. Through extensive testing using real-world and synthetic datasets, including fMRI data, our model demonstrates superior accuracy, efficiency, and generalizability compared to existing methods, making it a highly scalable and versatile solution for a wide range of applications involving complex, changing systems.

Animals move through their environments to gather food, avoid danger, and find mates, making locomotion a key trait for biological agents. Although this trait has been used in various ways, researching and developing methods to identify it in the wild is crucial. A new approach, grounded in Bayesian inference, analyzes sensory inputs to detect locomotion by estimating a key variable and its uncertainty. This approach has been applied to a standard dataset and shows comparable results to the best existing methods, while also being more efficient in computational terms. Furthermore, the new model's parameters can be easily adjusted to optimize performance, unlike other efficient methods that require complex modeling. Additionally, the new approach can incorporating outside information, offering several advantages over current leading models.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis and comparative analysis reveal that NN meets sufficient conditions for convergence and convergence rate, outperforming NN with an inception depth less than one. Furthermore, we identify the optimal inception depth that maximizes the convergence rate. Despite its benefits, we found that NN achieves performance comparable to other leading iterative methods at an inception depth of 1. To address this limitation, we propose two enhanced variants of NN with improved convergence rates, applicable to matrix inversion in a wide range of large dense matrix inputs at an inception depth of 1 for GPU acceleration.

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our results demonstrate that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also providing insights into the origin of the topological phenomenon induced by disorder. This investigation offers valuable information relevant to topological phenomena in biological systems and DNA.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve definitions across different contexts, including the analysis of local singularities, the investigation of the Feynman parameter space, and the exploration of the projective space via the Feynman parameters. Furthermore, the research highlights an intriguing implication: the Feynman parameter space features two distinct points at infinity, which, when incorporated into the Feynman space, enable the identification of a non-trivial 4-cycle within the surface. Additionally, the study demonstrates how the contours of the Feynman amplitude can be modified to yield a well-defined expression for the amplitude in the far-infrared limit, which is proportional to the logarithm of the ratio of the temperatures involved, thereby providing a fresh perspective on the calculation of the photon emissivity of a charged particle within thermal bath, as described by the Feynman diagram in figure 1.

This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge is particularly evident in the study of communication-efficient algorithms, specifically for distributing this model across a network where context information is shared among a cluster of agents. This context sharing assumption is suitable for certain applications, but not others. For instance, it does not accurately reflect a situation where the context is unique to each arm and an individual agent interacts with the system for just one arm. To better represent this latter scenario, a novel algorithmic challenge is considered: learning a contextual linear bandit in a distributed setting without context sharing, where each agent learns with local context that is not shared with others. It is shown that contextual linear bandits can be effectively learned in this situation using a contextual soft-elimination algorithm that achieves a regret bound of O(d log T) for T time steps and d dimensionality, with a poly(d, log T) multiplicative factor. This result is notable given its independence from the number of agents and the amount of communication used. The proposed method is also theoretically and practically demonstrated to be effective through numerical simulations and real-world data sets.

(2020), both enhancing policy evaluation and optimization through efficient policy value estimation and estimation-based methods, respectively. Building on Chang et al. (2020), Chen and Hu (2020) estimates distributional treatment rule parameters for improved robustness, similarly, on top of PSM-DTR of Kallus (2020), we incorporate DR uncertainty sets into estimates and prove a robust DTR learning guarantee.

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.
