Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions on a subset of documents, while human annotators manually review and correct the model's output in the form of JSON labels for documents it predicts incorrectly. This selective labeling process can be easily scaled to other types of documents including contracts, agreements, and forms. Our evaluation shows thatvisually based document extraction models gained higher F-scores with less than 1% of the usual labeling requirements, while the EXA model achieved comparable performance to one gaining the same training data set with a full labeled dataset on synthetic documents contracts. On two publicly available data sets our trained model achieved comparable performance to 83.8% and 76.9% of the state-of-the-art in terms of F-scores on the CV Document Extraction Library and Amazon Retrieve and Extract data set respectively.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches rely on template-based methods, which, although precise, are too slow for real-time processing. This paper introduces a machine learning approach using a XGBoost classifier for real-time classification of neutron star and black hole events and a deep learning convolutional neural network for electromagnetic analysis prediction. The proposed model achieves near-perfect accuracy in distinguishing between the two types of mergers and correctly predicts the spin of the neutron star in binary neutron star mergers and some of the black holes in mixed events with high confidence.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop in urban interactions of approximately 26% and finds that users with lower incomes experienced larger decreases than those with higher incomes. This disparity is maintained even with COVID-positive testing, indicating possible lasting impacts. Furthermore, although technological advancements may exacerbate income-related decreases in face-to-face interactions, policy measures like public transportation promotion could help mitigate them. The findings highlight the pandemic's potential to alter the economic benefits associated with urban settings, emphasizing the need for careful management of face-to-social interactions to avoid undesirable long-term consequences.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on the central star. Only the collapse of dense structures within starforming regions or on the inner edges of accretion disks can produce the observed effects of accretion bursts. Furthermore, high-velocity collisions between objects can also produce similar effects. Such events can transfer a substantial amount of mass to the star, possibly resulting in observable effects such as broad emission lines. These findings suggest that further studies using multi-dimensional models incorporating magnetic fields and chemistry can provide better insights into a possible link between the collapse of structure in molecular clouds and recently observed variations in massive young stellar bodies.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity, including cases where it outperforms their approach.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within this specific context.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing methods like optical cameras and laser scanners may struggle to provide reliable data for safe route planning. This paper introduces the Layered Navigation Controller framework, which integrates multiple real-world sensors to guide mobile robots in real time. This controller framework comprises four distinct modules, each responsible for a specific navigation task and executed sequentially. One of the key innovations presented is the real-time fusion of time-of-flight data from ceiling-mounted LiDAR and optical data from ground-mounted cameras to enhance depth perception and object recognition. Additionally, the system leverages visual odometry to enhance the precision of robot localization and employs a ReSCA-based module for obstacle detection and map segmentation. By combining these sensing technologies, the Layered Navigation Controller enables mobile robots to navigate safely and efficiently in various indoor environments.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the algorithm's step size meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $1g$ sensitivity of atomic interferometry, even sub-nT range expelled fields can be precisely measured. A theoretically derived formula for gradient sensitivity is relevant for scalable atomic sensor design, facilitating the creation of highly precise devices capable of measuring nanoscale phenomena in quantum physics and redefining the limits in studying quantum-classical boundary interactions in physics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture weights. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data structure to minimize memory access patterns, and a computation offloading mechanism to maximize GPU utilization.  Experimental evaluations showed that DynaSOAr outperformed leading GPU alternatives by a significant margin, achieving up to 10 times greater efficiency in memory allocation and a 1.6 times improvement in overall program execution time for five real-world SMMO applications.  Our findings also demonstrated that DynaSOAr could provide substantial performance gains of up to 46% over manually optimized code in five different test cases.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the slight shifting of YSR-state peaks was explained, and for Mn dimers, splitting patterns were identified and analyzed.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery from this dataset, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the stellar parameters for TOI-712 were determined, revealing it as a 1.2 solar radius, 1.0 solar mass, and 420 million years old G-type star. Previous research on this star has been limited as only one confirmed and four unconfirmed candidates were reported. Using a robust approach, we confirmed a new mini-Neptune named TOI-712.01, located at a very short 0.95-day period. The complete TOI-The least dense planet in this system, TOI-712.03, is found to extend towards its habitable zone at a semi-major axis of 0.384 AU. The TOI-712 system offers an intriguing target for future research, especially with the advent of the $TESS$ mission capable of discovering new interesting systems for potential local Earth-like worlds.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2 using a precise calculation method based on the spin-polarized density functional theory. This study utilized the linear augmented plane wave within the projector augmented wave framework. We found that carbon substitutions for titanium or oxygen atoms, as well as for Ti positions, lead to localized magnetic moments in both directions. In contrast, nitrogen defects in certain directions did not exhibit localization. We determined that both (N)_Ti and C defects exhibit directional bonding characteristics in specific directions. Additionally, we determined that the number of electrons played a crucial role in determining the magnitude of the localized magnetic moments for some defects. This study also explored possible mechanisms that could give rise to heterostructures with novel magnetic properties and suggested potential applications in spintronic devices.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, which is based on the size of the smallest set of vertices required to break all edges of any graph resembling $F$ with the largest possible edge coverage. This finding generalizes a discovery made by Schwebel's 3-coloring analogue and is comparable to a conjecture proposed by Gerencsér and Gyárfás two-coloring analogue. Additionally, we examine specific cases of this lower bound, provide a solution to a question posed by Gerencsér and Gyárfás, and provide insights into questions posed by Chen, Li, and Montellano.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding error tolerance when employing Toffoli gates error-mitigated through QSP and randomized compiling. This research particularly emphasizes the potential advantage of noise tolerance when dealing with decoherence, demonstrating that moving to qudits results in a more manageable increase in Toffoli gate counts while enhancing variance stability for measurement outcomes, thereby facilitating the application of Pauli diagonal measurements, which can be executed directly on physical qudits and avoid the need for additional gate operations and measurements required for measurement in the computational basis of qubits, ultimately providing a more efficient and tolerant approach for large-scale quantum simulations.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently generated through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons generated via this process remain unknown due to insufficient data on the contributing parameters. By leveraging high-intensity lasers paired with microscopic targets, a sufficient amount of polarization is achieved for the produced positrons. Our theoretical model accounts for the effects of electron and photon scattering, as well as the impact of angle and photon energy on the resulting polarization. The behavior of polarization in various situations is examined and the experimental requirements necessary to detect these positrons are outlined.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible size of S, whose elements can be multiplied in any order to produce every element of G, is known as the diameter of (G,S). Building on a breakthrough by umpyu and Tao, this paper explores the condition for a group G to have a small, bounded diameter relative to a generating set's size, specifically focusing on finite groups and providing a characterization and an effective version of this condition. Furthermore, it lists and examines several properties of the set of groups that meet this condition, and to illustrate, it incorporates some content from the study of the Erdo?s--Saharon Shelah simple group.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The module also includes a high-resolution digital-to-analog converter, an analog front-end, a digital temperature counter, and a control and calibration unit. The proposed temperature sensor module operates across a broad range of supply voltages (from 0.6V to 1.8V), with a corresponding frequency range of 5.51kHz to 45.1kHz at the lowest and highest points. The module's temperature resolution and operational span are 0.24{\deg}C and {-45.8{\deg}C} to 85{\deg}C, respectively. The sensor's inaccuracy and daily drift are 1.4{\deg}C and 0.06{\deg}C per day, while the daily consumption per temperature conversion is 1.06nJ.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2004.00461] and [arXiv:2004.00463], the project examines three key constructs: connections on principal bundle stacks, gerbes with connection over differential stacks, and Cartan connections over Lie groupoids. The primary objective is to associated contractible principal bundle stacks with any principal bundle stack, provide concrete realizations of certain higher fiber bundles with specific properties, and provide concrete realizations of Cartan bundle connections.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of newly formed stars.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the impact of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, surface breakage, and adhesion-breakage. The coefficients of static and dynamic friction are influenced by the characteristics of the surface. In a range of intermediate roughness, the coefficients of static and dynamic friction are approximately 0.75 and 0.55, respectively. However, for surfaces with higher levels of roughness, the coefficients increase to 1.5 and 0.95, respectively. As the level of roughness decreases, surface breakage gives way to a different phenomenon known as "plowing," resulting in an increase in friction. Furthermore, we observed that the angle of internal friction for dry liquid foams is around 65 degrees.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach for classifying the anomalous segment. Our findings demonstrated improvements over the baseline, achieving 66.3% and 72.3% for tasks 1 and 2, respectively.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability, leading to elastic finger formations. Notably, the membrane's slow recoil after finger retraction results in the outer fluid being trapped within the membrane's folds, effectively altering the fluid density contrast and allowing for that ratio to be deduced from membrane behavior. Notably observable, this phenomenon could have implications in geological settings where thick sediment layers are folded and rolled up, and in the business world, where it might influence decisions related to subsea farming, aquaculture, and turbine installations. Notwithstanding the membrane's slow rotation induces asymmetrical finger formations on either side of the cell's axis of symmetry and, it also allows the direction of formation to be dictated by the density contrast, buoyancy, and Coriolis force. In addition the study delves into the membrane's dynamics in the gradual stages of the system's rotation-induced formation and the capture of fluid droplets at the tip of the membrane fingers occurs as it retracts.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that only source sentences are considered by the attention mechanism, despite the fact that generated target words can also provide valuable information for subsequent word generation. In response, our proposed novel approach, generation attention, allows the model to be aware of previously generated words by dynamically learning additional projections for each attention input, thereby facilitating more informed decisions in word generation. Our model demonstrates superior performance over the standard approach in terms of BLEU scores on the Microsoft CrossArray and Facebook Tilt datasets.

The significant disparity in scales between biological and astronomical phenomena led Carl Sagan to suggest a translatational method for comprehending "middle" sizes. This perspective forms the basis for a more in-depth examination of the progression of grid computing. By analyzing primary sources including scholarly publications, books, web pages, and personal accounts, the author traces the development of grid computing and its underlying technologies. This analysis reveals how the initial framework and language of grid computing were shaped by the terminology of distributed computing, and how the scale of its applications forced a shift from a translatational method to a more direct, albeit costly, implementation. This perspective also provides an explanation for the distinct progression of computing terms from distributed to parallel to cloud computing.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model could potentially represent the combined essence of dark energy and matter as one substance under non-equilibrium conditions, and makes testable predictions that can be verified or refuted within a reasonable timescale. Several unified models have been proposed thus far, but a definitive explanation remains elusive. A DD (Drage Draper) model has been proposed that offers a testable unified model, but it lacks an anisotropic stress component. Because this component has been found to be non-negligible in recent studies, an anisotropic and dissipative version of the model has been developed to better reflect the non-equilibrium nature of the universe on a fundamental level. An anisotropic and unified dark fluid version of the Drage Draper model has been developed, and its impact on cosmological parameters has been examined, along with the evolution and power spectrum of unified dark matter and photons.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a specific dark matter model involving the J/ψ decay into light dark matter plus a photon. By analyzing J/ψ factory data from the Belle and Belle II experiments, we place new, stringent limits on light dark sector parameters and future data from Belle II will further refine these constraints, offering a comprehensive strategy to explore the light dark sector using e+e- colliders. Additionally, we derive constraints on the neutrino photon effective operator and find that Belle II has the capability to probe the neutrino scalar and tensor operators at levels unattainable by current experiments.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1,t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a walk that is defined by finitely many i.i.d. increment values. The parameter $\phi(x,b)$ is determined by the probability $\mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$ where $\kappa(x,b) = \frac{\sqrt{1-x}b-\sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x}b+\sqrt{1+x}}$ with $b = b_S \geq 0$ indicating the relative magnitude between positive and negative excursions of the random walk.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study has been undertaken to clarify the plasma source's operating modes, determine its sheath width, and assess its capability to produce helicon mode plasma at the highest possible density. Analysis of plasma source data revealed the transition from low frequency to high frequency discharge mode, and confirmed the presence of helicon mode at plasma densities below 5 x 10^11 m^-2, supported by comparisons with theoretical models and previous research.

While gold-standard pathology is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it's been hindered by low efficiency, difficulty in distinguishing between normal and malignant cells, and the time-consuming nature of the process. To address these issues and enhance diagnosis speed, accuracy, and capability, the development of deep-learning-based algorithms for identifying and delineating nuclei in histopathology images is essential for enabling two classes of algorithms, including convolutional neural networks, to be effectively deployed in real-world settings. Nevertheless, current research into nucleus segmentation has problems with accurately detecting nuclei in small images and failing to distinguish between healthy and cancerous nuclei in detailed images. To overcome these limitations and their impact on image analysis, we propose a novel framework for efficient and thorough nucleus detection in digital pathology images, referred to as the W-Net model, which features an initial conversion stage and an inverse refinement stage, and incorporates an attention mechanism in a specific module of the inverse refinement stage to prioritize the detection and segmentation of nuclei. In addition to its limitations in detecting nuclei in small images and its inability to differentiate between healthy and cancerous nuclei in detailed images, the W-Net model excels in addressing and overcoming these challenges for a wide range of nucleus segmentation image datasets, excelling in performance when compared to the U-Net model and other leading methods in terms of mean average precision, recall, and Dice similarity coefficient.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their findings.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. Without an anisotropic stress correction, the resulting field equations cannot produce a stable solution. However, this transformation enables us to describe specific fields - rotating hairy black holes and flat space solitons - in the context of Maxwell's and ANSOHN-Mansfield theories. Additionally, we can derive a constant, stress correctd model by taking a specific constraint on the coupling constants, allowing for the existence of rotating hairy black holes even in this simplified scenario. This particular stress correctd model can also produce rotating solitons under certain conditions, as well as other types of solitons found in the original, uncoupled field theories, which can persist in a linearized approximation of the Stueckelberg-simplified model.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue mechanics and the precise measurement of tissue tumor strains. Non-linear convolution-based methods, in particular, provide precise strain estimates but have high computational costs, limiting their clinical use. This research introduces the virtual source synthetic aperture (SSA) approach to improve the computation of non-linear elastograms, achieving accurate lateral strain estimates and significant improvements in depth and frame rate. Furthermore, a ssA pre-computation approach is suggested to maintain accurate lateral estimates while improving frame rate. When compared to the non-linear FDK and slant stack methods, the SSA approach offers a 2.3x to 5.5x and 1.1x to 1.6x reduction in FLOPS and memory usage. In addition, the SSA approach provides unlimited depth extensions at the same frame rate and allows for increased frame rates with the same depth. ThessA pre-computation also shows a 2.1x to 4.4x reduction in FLOPS, allowing deeper investigations into tissue mechanics for effective ultrasound elastography.

Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with specific properties. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an innovative framework known as "logical pseudocodes," which we demonstrate by recreating and analyzing famous data structures and sorting methods, including the binary search, quicksort, b-trees, and the merge-knway sort, in conjunction with corresponding logical frameworks and operational strategies built upon monad transformations and pseudocode.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves integrating and testing the EEC set of Effective Event Generators, which calculate both single boson radiation and weak boson fusion distribution functions and cross-sections, in a unified framework for the simulation of beyond-standard-model particle interactions via t-channel weak boson exchanges in high-energy lepton colliders.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion, particularly when the environment
structures are significantly different. To mitigate this issue and take full
advantage of the potential benefits of a shared model, we introduce a modular
dynamics network that allows each task to have its own submodule while keeping
the number of parameters constant. Our approach demonstrates superior or at least
comparable multi-task reinforcement learning performance when using a single
modular dynamics network, and allows for seamless switching between networks as
new tasks are introduced.

In 1936, Alfred Tarstein developed a modified version of his original proof to counter alternative proposals for formal systems that could detect true statements, specifically addressing suggestions made by Jacques Bernays and Carl Hempel. This adjusted approach, utilizing the features of a logical framework, demonstrated how to construct statements within the same system that it could accurately assess, thereby differing from earlier proofs based on foundational inconsistencies, which were based on premises considered too flawed to rely on.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is often solvable by finding the probability distribution of possible images and making decisions based on that distribution. A key challenge is efficiently sampling from this probability distribution. To address this, we look for ways to quickly generate samples that accurately reflect the true distribution. In this paper, we develop a novel method using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN to accelerate the calculation of the probability distribution and generate samples. The method is designed to be compact and adaptable, allowing it to process large-scale images. To enhance the speed of the algorithm, we create a compact network structure and a time-varying penalty that limits the size of the samples. The resulting method is highly efficient, capable of generating 1024x1024 images in under a second while closely matching the true probability distribution.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions under which specific systems exhibit invariant behavior. Specifically, we outline the requirements for systems with invariant lines and planes. We also explore the fractionation of variables in these systems, assessing the impact on line and plane invariance. Through a series of examples, we demonstrate the difficulty of achieving invariance in fractional systems and prove non-existence of invariant line and plane systems under certain conditions. Finally, we extend our proof to show non-existence of invariant sets in fractional systems.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens that disrupt the signals of distant radio pulsars, a characteristic of pulsar timing, and has been utilized in previous studies to analyze these screens in detail. This research focuses on investigating two specific screens discovered through analysis of the pulsar B1133+16, and has been facilitated by improved data and a more comprehensive model of the pulsar's orbit around the galaxy. As the pulsar moves in its path, the pulsar signals travel through the galaxy and can be affected by plasma effects such as pulsar beam deflection and the changing total electron content of the interstellar medium, and this research has been supported by the use of long-term timing data from various volunteers, and allows for the determination of changes in electron content as the pulsar moves around the galaxy, and this is compared to simulations of the interstellar medium, and this research reveals varying densities of electrons around the galaxy and may be attributed to plasma waves known as Langmuir waves, and this research holds particular relevance to the interstellar medium in our galaxy and other spiral galaxies throughout the universe.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch plan projections that are suboptimal in the feature space. In contrast, this paper introduces the concept of a quasi-periodic function to further WN and derives a novel network architecture based on this function. The proposed model shares the same hyperparameters and network depth as WN for comparison purposes. In a synthetic speech generation task, the proposed Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) outperforms the baseline WaveNet (WN) by 10% in Fréchet Speech Generation Quality (FSGQ) and 40% in Mean Opinion Score (MOS). In addition, the control of the proposed model on the pitch range is 2.5 times greater than that of the baseline WN. The source code is available at https://github.com/Doostabadi/QPNet-.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources derived from Flickr, on which VGG-Sound Source is evaluated, demonstrating that our approach outperforms previous methods.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighborhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-like graphs with minimal performance loss for other graphs.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in both outcome magnitude and delay, drawing on the fourth order
Tsallis delay discounting model. Our approach allows us to examine the
relationship between the parameters of this model and those of the widely
used dual process model of delay discounting. We find that the parameters
of our model map onto the parameters of the dual process model in a one-to-one
magnetic fashion, indicating that our model inherently incorporates both
systematic and intuitive thinking. Furthermore, by integrating and extending
prior research, we determine the conditions under which individuals may
incorrectly prioritize shorter delays due to the interaction between
immediate gratification and thinking patterns. We also investigate the
influence of ambient temperature on preference reversals, thereby proposing
a new experimental design for such studies.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic factor as a direct consequence of the equilibrium state's Gaussian nature.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet the dark matter relic abundance conditions, considering both its tree-level and higher-order interactions. Additionally, we assess the stability of the holographic effective potential and the theory's capacity to explain the solar neutrino data. However, we find the model falls short in addressing light neutrino mass patterns and dark matter charged-current interactions.

We employ exact diagonalization to investigate the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal field environment specific to transition metal oxides. Through direct computation, we derive the effective Hamiltonian's parameters, including those resulting from moderate to strong correlations. Our study yields the characteristic energy splitting between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals under various conditions. Consequently, our research provides actionable insights for interpreting experimental data related to $d$-electron systems.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the medical field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated with minimal risk to patient safety. Researchers were able to produce a GAN-based approach to counteracting over-regularization issues in neural network models, which inadvertently suppress distinct feature patterns associated with diseases. By examining chest X-ray data for pneumonia detection and cancer, this study evaluated network limitations and demonstrated the practicality of network outputs in clinical diagnosis. The study also explored network limitations in certain network regions and demonstrated practical utility in network-assisted cancer diagnosis.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies.
